title: Compare Dotted Version Strings
statement:
A version string is a list of non-negative whole numbers separated by dots, such as "2.10.3". Each part is compared as a number, so leading zeros do not matter: "01" and "1" are equal. If one version has fewer parts, its missing parts count as 0.

Compare v1 and v2 part by part from the left. Return -1 if v1 is older (smaller), 1 if it is newer, and 0 if they are equal.

examples.why: 10 > 9 as numbers. Comparing the strings as text would say "2.10" < "2.9".
The missing parts of "3" count as 0, so both are 3.0.0.
002 equals 2, so the first two parts tie. The third part is 0 against 1.

constraints: Both strings contain only digits and dots, with no empty parts
Every part fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Splitting on dots and comparing parts one by one is the core. What do you do when one list runs out first?
Turn each part into a number before comparing, so leading zeros disappear and 10 beats 9.
Walk both strings with two indexes, reading one number at a time from each (0 if that string is exhausted). Stop at the first difference.

explain.intuition:
This is the comparison a package manager makes when it decides whether 2.10.0 is newer than 2.9.4. Text comparison gets it wrong, because "1" < "9" character by character. Each dot-separated part has to be read as a number.

Pad the shorter version with zeros and compare parts left to right; the first unequal part decides. You can do that without building arrays: keep one index in each string, parse digits until the next dot, and treat an exhausted string as producing zeros.
steps: While either index is inside its string: read the number at i in v1 (digits until a dot or the end, 0 if already past the end), then skip the dot. Do the same at j in v2.
If the two numbers differ, return -1 or 1.
If both strings run out without a difference, return 0.
pitfalls: Comparing the parts as strings: "10" < "9" as text.
Treating "1.0" and "1" as different because the part counts differ.
Converting the whole string to a float: "1.10" would equal "1.1" and lose the second dot entirely.

solutions.title: Split and pad
solutions.idea: Split both strings on dots, convert parts to numbers and compare position by position, using 0 past the end of the shorter list.

solutions.title: Two pointers, parse on the fly
solutions.idea: Read one number at a time from each string. A finished string keeps yielding 0.

followups: Support pre-release tags like 1.2.0-beta.2, where a tagged version is older than the plain one. How does the comparison change?
Sort a list of 100 000 versions. Would you parse each comparison again or precompute keys?
